B-01.04.title: Extend to complex numbers
B-01.04.summary: Find roots that do not exist over the reals.
B-01.04.when: A real quadratic has a negative discriminant.
hypotheses: Complex solutions are permitted by the problem.
B-01.04.guarantees: Every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root.
B-01.04.pitfalls: Changing the domain changes the problem: a complex root is not a real solution.
steps: Isolate the square.
Use i² = −1 and keep both roots.
Substitute both roots into the original equation.

B-01.07.title: Complete an inner product space
B-01.07.summary: Add the missing limits of Cauchy sequences.
B-01.07.when: A space has geometry but is not complete in its induced norm.
hypotheses: A positive definite inner product is defined
Use its induced norm for completion.
B-01.07.guarantees: A dense isometric embedding into a Hilbert space, unique up to isometry.
B-01.07.pitfalls: L² convergence need not imply convergence at every point.
steps: The limit is a discontinuous step function (up to a null set).
The error tends to zero; the limit belongs to L².

B-02.01.title: Factor an expression
B-02.01.summary: Turn a polynomial into a product of simpler factors.
B-02.01.when: You need the roots of a polynomial or a useful cancellation.
hypotheses: Factorization is an identity over the chosen field
For the zero-product rule, work over a field such as ℝ or ℂ.
B-02.01.guarantees: The polynomial and its factorization have the same values and roots.
B-02.01.pitfalls: Canceling a factor in a fraction still requires excluding its zeros.
steps: Find two numbers with sum −5 and product 6.
A product is zero only if a factor is zero.
Check both roots in the original polynomial.

B-02.02.title: Collect terms & isolate
B-02.02.summary: Combine like terms and isolate an unknown.
hypotheses: Add the same expression to both sides
Divide only by a known nonzero coefficient.
B-02.02.guarantees: Reversible steps preserve the solution set.
B-02.02.pitfalls: If the coefficient is zero, distinguish an identity from a contradiction.
steps: Subtract 6 from both sides.
Divide by 3, which is nonzero.
Verify by substitution.

B-02.03.title: Complete the square
B-02.03.summary: Rewrite a quadratic as a shifted square.
B-02.03.when: Factoring is difficult, or you want to see the discriminant.
hypotheses: The quadratic coefficient a is nonzero
Choose the required real or complex domain.
B-02.03.guarantees: An exact identity leading to the quadratic formula.
B-02.03.pitfalls: Keep both square-root signs; a negative discriminant has no real roots.
steps: Add 9 after moving the constant.
Recognize the perfect square.
Take both square roots and isolate x.
Check both solutions.

B-02.04.title: Clear denominators
B-02.04.summary: Replace a rational equation with a polynomial on its domain.
B-02.04.when: Fractions hide a simpler polynomial equation.
hypotheses: Record every original denominator
Exclude their zeros before multiplying.
B-02.04.guarantees: Equivalent equations on the restricted domain.
B-02.04.pitfalls: Simplification must not restore excluded inputs.
steps: Record the original denominator restriction.
Find candidates from the numerator.
Discard 1; only −1 satisfies the original equation.

B-02.05.title: Divide with a case split
B-02.05.summary: Separate the zero case before canceling an unknown factor.
B-02.05.when: You are about to divide by a variable expression.
hypotheses: The divisor must be nonzero on the branch where division is used.
B-02.05.guarantees: The union of the zero and nonzero branches preserves all solutions.
B-02.05.pitfalls: Dividing by x immediately loses the possible root x = 0.
steps: Bring all terms to one side and factor.
Treat the zero factor and the nonzero branch.
Both roots satisfy the original equation.

B-02.06.title: Square both sides
B-02.06.summary: Remove a radical and generate candidate solutions.
hypotheses: For real square roots, the radicand is nonnegative
Check the sign of the other side
Verify all candidates in the original equation.
B-02.06.guarantees: Every original solution survives squaring; the converse needs checking.
steps: The square root is nonnegative, so x must be too.
Square to obtain candidates 2 and −1.
Reject −1 and verify 2 in the original equation.

B-02.07.title: Substitute a new variable
B-02.07.summary: Reveal a familiar equation inside an unfamiliar one.
B-02.07.when: Repeated powers or a repeated expression hide a simpler structure.
hypotheses: Track the range of the substitution
Recover every permitted original value from each new value.
B-02.07.guarantees: An equivalent problem when the range and inverse branches are retained.
B-02.07.pitfalls: For u = x² over ℝ, negative u has no preimage and positive u usually has two.
steps: Replace the repeated square by u.
Factor the quadratic.
Invert x² = 1 and x² = 4, keeping both signs.
All four candidates satisfy the original even polynomial.

B-02.08.title: Gaussian elimination
B-02.08.summary: Use reversible row operations to solve linear systems.
hypotheses: Swap rows, add multiples, or scale by a nonzero number
Track pivots and any parameter cases.
B-02.08.guarantees: An equivalent linear system with the same solution set.
B-02.08.pitfalls: A zero pivot may require a row swap; a zero row does not automatically mean inconsistency.
steps: Eliminate x from the second row.
Back-substitute into the first equation.
Check both equations.

B-03.05.title: Fubini & Tonelli
B-03.05.summary: Replace a product integral by iterated integrals.
B-03.05.when: A multivariable integral becomes easier one variable at a time.
hypotheses: Measurability on σ-finite product measure spaces
Fubini: absolute integrability
Tonelli: nonnegative integrand, possibly infinite integral.
B-03.05.guarantees: The iterated and product integrals agree under the appropriate theorem.
B-03.05.pitfalls: Conditional convergence alone does not justify exchanging integration order.
steps: The integrand is continuous and nonnegative on a compact square.
The product integrand and product domain allow factorization.
Direct iterated integration confirms the value.

B-03.07.title: Separate variables
B-03.07.summary: Turn a separable differential equation into two integrals.
B-03.07.when: The derivative is a product of a function of x and a function of y.
hypotheses: Work where h(y) is nonzero
Check constant solutions h(y) = 0 separately
Retain initial conditions and solution intervals.
B-03.07.guarantees: An implicit solution on each valid branch.
steps: On the nonzero branch, separate the variables.
Integrate and exponentiate; y = 0 is also an equilibrium.
The initial condition selects K = 1; verify the derivative.

B-03.12.title: Diagonalize a normal matrix
B-03.12.summary: Decouple a linear operator into orthogonal eigenmodes.
B-03.12.when: Powers or coupled linear systems are difficult in the current basis.
hypotheses: A is a finite-dimensional complex normal matrix: A*A = AA*.
B-03.12.guarantees: A unitary eigenbasis exists; Hermitian matrices have real eigenvalues.
B-03.12.pitfalls: Not every matrix is diagonalizable, or unitarily diagonalizable.
steps: Choose orthonormal eigenvectors of this symmetric matrix.
Verify the two eigenvalues directly.
The transformed operator acts separately on each coordinate.

B-03.13.title: Fourier series
B-03.13.summary: Represent a periodic L² function by orthonormal modes.
B-03.13.when: You need frequency coordinates or a finite-mode approximation.
hypotheses: f belongs to L²([−π, π])
Use the complete basis eₙ(x) = exp(inx)/√(2π).
B-03.13.guarantees: The series converges in L² norm and Parseval preserves energy.
B-03.13.pitfalls: L² convergence does not guarantee convergence everywhere or uniformly.
steps: Euler’s identity gives exactly two modes.
Account for the normalized basis.
Verify Parseval by integrating cos² on [−π, π].

B-04.01.title: Use polar coordinates
B-04.01.summary: Expose radial symmetry and simplify planar integrals.
B-04.01.when: The expression depends on x² + y² or the region is circular.
hypotheses: Choose a domain that handles angle branches and the origin
Use the Jacobian r for area integrals.
B-04.01.guarantees: An equivalent coordinate description with the correct measure.
B-04.01.pitfalls: Forgetting the Jacobian changes the integral.
steps: The disk becomes a rectangle in (r, θ) parameters.
Include r and integrate; this agrees with the disk area.

B-04.05.title: Fourier transform
B-04.05.summary: Turn differentiation into multiplication in frequency.
B-04.05.when: A constant-coefficient differential operator is hard to invert.
hypotheses: For the classical derivative rule, sufficient regularity and decay
Use a function space and inversion theorem appropriate to the problem.
B-04.05.guarantees: Under f̂(ξ) = ∫f(x)e^(−iξx) dx, derivatives become algebraic multipliers.
B-04.05.pitfalls: Boundary conditions, multiplier zeros and inverse-transform hypotheses still matter.
steps: Transform the second derivative with the stated convention.
The multiplier never vanishes on the real axis.
Verify in frequency; invert in a suitable space, for example for Schwartz data.

B-04.06.title: Convolution to multiplication
B-04.06.summary: Replace a convolution integral by a pointwise product.
B-04.06.when: A linear filter or integral equation contains a convolution.
hypotheses: For the standard classical theorem, f and g are in L¹(ℝ)
Fix the Fourier normalization.
B-04.06.guarantees: The transform of a convolution equals the product of transforms.
B-04.06.pitfalls: The transform of a product is a convolution with a normalization factor.
steps: Direct integration runs from 0 to x when x ≥ 0.
Direct transforms verify the convolution identity.

B-04.07.title: Laplace transform
B-04.07.summary: Solve an initial-value ODE in an algebraic domain.
B-04.07.when: An ODE has initial data and a useful Laplace transform.
hypotheses: Suitable regularity and exponential order
Work in a half-plane of convergence
Retain initial data in derivative transforms.
B-04.07.guarantees: The transformed equation encodes the ODE together with its initial value.
B-04.07.pitfalls: Dropping the initial-value term changes the problem.
steps: Transform the equation with y(0) = 0.
Solve algebraically and decompose into partial fractions.
Invert and verify the ODE and initial value.

B-04.11.title: Euler’s identity
B-04.11.summary: Connect rotations, trigonometry and complex exponentials.
B-04.11.when: Trigonometric products or rotations are awkward.
hypotheses: θ is real in the geometric interpretation
Angles are identified modulo 2π for a unit complex number.
B-04.11.guarantees: An exact identity converting trigonometric and exponential expressions.
B-04.11.pitfalls: The argument is not a globally unique inverse of the complex exponential.
steps: Expand the product using Euler’s identity.
Compare real parts to recover the addition formula.
Check a concrete pair of angles.

B-05.01.title: Use the complex conjugate
B-05.01.summary: Connect complex arithmetic to nonnegative real quantities.
B-05.01.when: You need to divide complex numbers or compute a modulus.
hypotheses: For inversion, z is nonzero
Conjugation is antilinear over ℂ.
B-05.01.guarantees: Multiplication by the conjugate gives the squared modulus.
B-05.01.pitfalls: Conjugating a complex scalar also conjugates any coefficient multiplying it.
steps: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.
The denominator is the squared modulus.
Multiplication verifies the reciprocal.

B-05.03.title: Hermitian inner product
B-05.03.summary: Build positive geometry on complex vectors.
B-05.03.when: The naive bilinear dot product gives a negative squared length.
hypotheses: Vectors belong to the same complex inner product space
This atlas uses linearity in the second argument.
B-05.03.guarantees: Conjugate symmetry, positive definiteness and a real nonnegative squared norm.
B-05.03.pitfalls: Other books use the opposite convention; projection formulas must match.
steps: Conjugate the first vector before multiplying.
The squared norm is positive.
The inner product certifies orthogonality and length.

B-05.04.title: Orthogonal projection
B-05.04.summary: Find the closest point on a line using an inner product.
B-05.04.when: You need a best approximation or an orthogonal decomposition.
hypotheses: u is nonzero
Use a consistent inner product convention.
B-05.04.guarantees: The residual is orthogonal to u and the projection minimizes the distance to v on span(u).
B-05.04.pitfalls: A projection loses information: the original vector cannot be recovered from it alone.
steps: Compute numerator and denominator using the conjugate.
The projection coefficient is 1.
Orthogonality verifies the best approximation.

B-05.06.title: Riesz representation
B-05.06.summary: Represent a continuous linear functional by a unique vector.
B-05.06.when: A functional is easier to understand geometrically.
hypotheses: H is a Hilbert space
F is linear and continuous
Use linearity in the second inner product argument.
B-05.06.guarantees: There is a unique representing vector v with ‖F‖ = ‖v‖.
B-05.06.pitfalls: An arbitrary normed space need not have this inner product representation.
steps: Choose v so its conjugated components are the coefficients of F.
Check the representation for an arbitrary vector x.

B-05.07.title: Adjoint operator
B-05.07.summary: Move an operator across the inner product.
B-05.07.when: You need self-adjointness, normality or an operator’s dual action.
hypotheses: A is a bounded linear operator on a Hilbert space
For matrices, use the Hermitian inner product.
B-05.07.guarantees: The adjoint exists uniquely; in finite dimensions it is the conjugate transpose.
B-05.07.pitfalls: For unbounded operators the adjoint’s domain is part of the definition.
steps: Transpose and conjugate every entry.
This identity verifies the defining inner product property.

B-06.03.title: Divergence theorem
B-06.03.summary: Replace boundary flux by a volume integral.
B-06.03.when: Parametrizing the boundary is harder than differentiating the field.
hypotheses: A bounded region with sufficiently regular boundary
A sufficiently regular vector field
Use the outward normal.
B-06.03.guarantees: The total outward flux equals the integral of divergence.
B-06.03.pitfalls: An inward normal reverses the flux sign.
steps: Differentiate the two components.
Multiply by the area of the unit disk.
Direct boundary integration confirms the result.

B-06.05.title: Residue theorem
B-06.05.summary: Turn a contour integral into a sum at poles.
B-06.05.when: Complex singularities simplify an otherwise difficult integral.
hypotheses: f is meromorphic inside and on a positively oriented simple closed contour
Only finitely many poles lie inside and none on the contour.
B-06.05.guarantees: The contour integral is determined by the enclosed residues.
B-06.05.pitfalls: For real improper integrals, justify contributions from added contour segments.
steps: The only pole inside the contour is simple.
Apply the theorem for counterclockwise orientation.
Uniform convergence on the circle allows termwise integration; only 1/z contributes.

B-07.02.title: Taylor polynomial with remainder
B-07.02.summary: Approximate a function while controlling the error.
B-07.02.when: A local polynomial is easier to calculate than the original function.
hypotheses: Sufficient differentiability on the interval between a and x
Bound the next derivative to control the Lagrange remainder.
B-07.02.guarantees: A finite polynomial plus an exact remainder; a derivative bound gives an error estimate.
B-07.02.pitfalls: Smoothness alone does not imply equality with the infinite Taylor series.
steps: Use the degree-two polynomial about 0.
On [0, 0.2], the third derivative is at most e^0.2.
The result is an interval, not an asserted exact decimal.

B-08.01.title: Dominated convergence
B-08.01.summary: Justify moving a limit inside an integral.
B-08.01.when: Pointwise limits are easy but integrals depend on n.
hypotheses: Measurable functions converge almost everywhere
One integrable g dominates every abs(fₙ) almost everywhere.
B-08.01.guarantees: The integrals converge and ‖fₙ − f‖₁ tends to zero.
B-08.01.pitfalls: A different bound for every n is insufficient: the dominator must be uniform.
steps: Convergence fails at x = 1 only, a null set; 1 is integrable.
Apply dominated convergence.
The explicit integral verifies the limit.

B-09.01.title: Intermediate value theorem
B-09.01.summary: Guarantee a real root by a change of sign.
B-09.01.when: You need to prove a root exists or bracket it for bisection.
hypotheses: f is continuous on [a, b]
Endpoint values have opposite signs.
B-09.01.guarantees: At least one root lies inside the interval.
B-09.01.pitfalls: A sign change across a discontinuity does not guarantee a root; uniqueness is not implied.
steps: The polynomial is continuous and changes sign.
Existence follows without a closed-form root.
An additional monotonicity argument proves uniqueness on this interval.

B-09.03.title: Banach fixed point theorem
B-09.03.summary: Turn a contraction into a unique solution and a convergent iteration.
B-09.03.when: An equation can be written x = T(x).
hypotheses: A nonempty complete metric space X
T maps all of X into X
A uniform contraction constant 0 ≤ q < 1.
B-09.03.guarantees: A unique fixed point; every iteration from X converges with an explicit error bound.
B-09.03.pitfalls: A small derivative at one point is not a uniform contraction estimate.
steps: Check invariance, completeness and a uniform contraction bound.
Iterate from any point of [0, 1].
This posterior bound certifies error, unlike decimal stability alone.

B-09.09.title: Lax–Milgram theorem
B-09.09.summary: Establish a unique weak solution in a Hilbert space.
B-09.09.when: A PDE is better expressed through test functions.
hypotheses: H is a real Hilbert space
a is bilinear, continuous and coercive
F is a continuous linear functional.
B-09.09.guarantees: There is a unique weak solution u in H.
B-09.09.pitfalls: A weak solution is not automatically a classical solution; extra regularity needs proof.
steps: Choose the Sobolev space and use its derivative norm.
Cauchy–Schwarz and Poincaré give continuity.
Coercivity gives a unique weak solution; the variational identity is its verification criterion.

B-10.02.title: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
B-10.02.summary: Bound an inner product by the product of lengths.
B-10.02.when: You need an estimate, continuity or an error bound.
hypotheses: A real or complex inner product space.
B-10.02.guarantees: A universal bound; equality exactly for linearly dependent vectors, including zero cases.
B-10.02.pitfalls: This is a bound, not a formula for the actual inner product.
steps: Compute the quantities in the bound.
Squaring nonnegative sides verifies the inequality.

B-11.05.title: Euler–Lagrange equation
B-11.05.summary: Find the differential equation of a stationary curve.
B-11.05.when: A problem asks for a curve minimizing an integral functional.
hypotheses: Sufficient regularity of the Lagrangian and candidate curve
Fixed endpoint variations vanish at the boundary
The candidate is an interior stationary point.
B-11.05.guarantees: A necessary stationarity equation; further conditions are needed for a minimum.
B-11.05.pitfalls: Solving Euler–Lagrange alone does not prove a global minimum.
steps: The stationary candidates are straight lines.
The endpoint values determine the line.
A separate nonnegative energy calculation verifies the global minimum.

B-11.06.title: Least squares by projection
B-11.06.summary: Project data onto the range of a matrix.
B-11.06.when: An overdetermined linear system has no exact solution.
hypotheses: Finite-dimensional real or complex Euclidean spaces
Full column rank is required for a unique coefficient vector.
B-11.06.guarantees: A best approximation exists and its residual is orthogonal to the column space.
B-11.06.pitfalls: Normal equations can worsen conditioning; QR or SVD is often preferable numerically.
steps: Solve the normal equation.
Orthogonality certifies the least-squares solution.
Completing the square directly verifies the unique minimum.

B-12.01.title: Bisection
B-12.01.summary: Repeatedly halve a bracket containing a real root.
B-12.01.when: You have a continuous function and a sign-changing interval.
hypotheses: Continuity on the initial closed interval
Opposite nonzero endpoint signs, or handle endpoint roots first.
B-12.01.guarantees: A nested root bracket; the midpoint error is at most half the interval width.
B-12.01.pitfalls: Without continuity a sign change can hide a pole instead of a root.
steps: The positive midpoint value keeps the left half.
The endpoint signs still differ.
The new midpoint has a certified error bound.

B-12.02.title: Newton’s method
B-12.02.summary: Follow tangent lines toward a root.
B-12.02.when: A differentiable equation has no convenient exact solution.
hypotheses: Nonzero derivative at each iterate
For local quadratic convergence, sufficient smoothness near a simple root and a sufficiently close initial guess.
B-12.02.guarantees: Under local hypotheses, fast convergence to a simple root.
B-12.02.pitfalls: Poor starting points, zero derivatives or multiple roots can spoil convergence.
steps: Insert f and its derivative into Newton’s rule.
Compute two iterates.
A residual plus the factorization of the error verifies progress.

B-12.09.title: Residual & conditioning
B-12.09.summary: Relate an approximate solution’s residual to its error.
B-12.09.when: A numerical answer seems accurate because the residual is small.
hypotheses: A is invertible
Use compatible matrix and vector norms
Estimate the inverse norm or condition number.
B-12.09.guarantees: A posterior error control that accounts for sensitivity.
B-12.09.pitfalls: A tiny residual can coexist with a large solution error in an ill-conditioned problem.
steps: The residual is very small.
Yet the actual error has size 1.
The inverse norm explains and bounds the error exactly here.

B-12.11.title: Verify in the original equation
B-12.11.summary: Check candidates against the original expression and domain.
B-12.11.when: A transformation, cancellation or symbolic engine produced roots.
hypotheses: The candidate lies in the original domain
Every original expression is defined
Exact substitution gives zero residual, or numerical error is controlled.
B-12.11.guarantees: Each checked candidate is a solution; completeness requires a separate argument.
B-12.11.pitfalls: A numerical residual near zero alone is not an exact proof or a complete root list.
steps: Substitute into the original equation, not the squared one.
Reject the extraneous root and verify the valid root 2.

ui.subtitle: An atlas for mathematical thinking
ui.search: Search a method, formula or obstacle…
ui.introTitle:
A different view.
A simpler problem.
ui.introText: Find the transformation that makes your problem click. Explore methods, check their conditions, and connect the ideas behind the equations.
ui.noResults: No bridges match these filters. Try another term or clear the filters.
ui.emptyPins: Pin a few bridges to keep them close and compare their approaches.
ui.example: Cross the bridge: a worked example
ui.catalogNote: A curated starting collection based on the founding atlas. More nodes can be added through the JSON catalog.
ui.compareText: Keep the purpose, conditions and guarantees in view while choosing your next step.
ui.compareEmpty: Pin at least two bridges to compare their methods.
ui.mapText: Expand nodes, zoom and follow a bridge link. Choose a family to focus on one part of the atlas.
ui.mapFallback: The same hierarchy is available in the accessible tree navigator.
ui.routesText: Each route connects a sequence of bridges. Start anywhere and return to the foundations when needed.
ui.solverText: Let Algebrite inspect an equation, suggest bridges, and explain supported solution steps. All calculations stay in your browser.
ui.syntax: Use explicit multiplication: 2*x. Powers: x^2. Functions: sqrt(x), sin(x), cos(x), tan(x), exp(x), log(x). One variable; polynomials up to degree 4 and simple radical equations have guided steps.
ui.noRestrictions: No additional restrictions from denominators or functions.
ui.emptyRoots: No solutions in the chosen domain.
ui.identity: Every value in the original domain satisfies this equation.
ui.unsupported: This form needs further analysis. These bridges are suggestions, not a certified solution path.
ui.limited: The guided solver handles single-variable polynomials of degree 1–4, rational equations with such numerators, and sqrt(polynomial) = linear polynomial. Other forms receive suggestions only.
ui.invalid: Enter one valid equation with one supported variable. Use explicit multiplication and supported function names.
ui.tooComplex: This expression is too large for the guided solver. Simplify it first.
ui.timeout: The calculation took too long and was stopped. Try a simpler expression.
ui.workerError: The symbolic engine could not finish this calculation. Try a simpler expression.
ui.stepNormalize: Move everything to the left and simplify.
ui.stepFactor: Factor the numerator. Denominator restrictions still apply.
ui.stepLinear: Isolate the variable using a nonzero coefficient.
ui.stepQuadratic: Use the quadratic formula; the discriminant determines real or complex roots.
ui.stepSubstitution: Recognize a quadratic in the squared variable, then recover both signs.
ui.stepRoots: Generate polynomial root candidates with Algebrite.
ui.stepSquare: Square both sides to generate candidates, then check the original radical equation.
ui.stepVerify: Substitute each candidate into both original sides and check every domain restriction.
ui.rootNote: Only candidates certified in the original equation are accepted. An uncertified candidate needs further checking; the displayed list may then be incomplete.
ui.footer: Know why. Check when. See what follows.
ui.copyFailed: Copy the address from your browser.
